Volume 08 · Chapter 02

Free cash flow and discounting

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v08-c01

By the endDerive cash flows to the firm and equity and choose consistent discount rates.

Capability and prerequisites

You can derive free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) and free cash flow to equity (FCFE), reconcile the values of the associated claims, and match discounting to the cash flow's date, purchasing-power unit, currency and financing policy. Use dated incremental cash flows and present value, the three statements, cash versus accounting tax, and linked financing forecasts. Discount rates here are supplied conditional assumptions. Their risk-based estimation belongs to Chapter 4.

A profitable business has income of 90, operating cash of 118 and a payment to shareholders of 88. Another analyst calls its free cash flow 109.5. These numbers can all be correct. The useful question is which investment and financing payments have already been deducted, who owns the remaining claim, and which tax convention produced it. Applying the same rate to every number does not resolve the difference.

1. Define the cash claim before discounting

Let t denote the end of an annual period. All amounts in a calculation use the same entity, currency and price basis. EBIT is operating profit before financing interest and income tax. D&A is the depreciation and amortization already deducted in EBIT. CapEx is cash investment in operating long-lived assets. W is noncash operating working capital, such as receivables plus inventory minus non-interest-bearing operating payables. Write ΔWt = Wt − Wt−1: a positive change absorbs cash. We keep cash, interest-bearing debt and income-tax balances out of W here and handle them separately.

FCFF measures operating cash after necessary reinvestment and taxes calculated without the interest deduction. It precedes payments to debt and equity. FCFE measures cash available to ordinary shareholders after the financing policy's interest, tax and net borrowing. The chapter's simple firm has no preferred shares, minority owners or other claims. More complicated ownership requires an explicit claim bridge. Damodaran's FCFF, FCFE and working-capital definitions provide the conventional starting distinctions; our cases below specify their own narrower assumptions and reconcile the amounts independently.

Items that need different treatment
ItemCash-flow consequence
Depreciation included in profitAdd it back in the profit-to-cash bridge; deduct the actual investment payment separately. The addback is not a new cash receipt.
Receivables or inventory increaseDeduct the operating investment, after the matching operating-payable movement. Sales are not necessarily collections.
New borrowing / principal repaymentChanges FCFE through net borrowing; neither is operating revenue or a deduction in FCFF.
InterestDeduct it when constructing the shareholder claim, using the actual associated tax effect. Keep it out of operating EBIT.
Retained excess cash or a separate investmentValue the asset and its eventual disposition consistently; do not count both the retained cash balance and the same cash as already distributed.

“Free” means after the reinvestment included in the forecast. It does not mean legally distributable, certain, or available without maintaining service capacity. FCFF can be negative while an investment is being built. FCFE can be negative even with positive FCFF if debt repayments are large. A financing shortfall needs an identified contribution, borrowing, asset sale or operating change; a positive terminal number cannot pay today's bill.

2. Derive FCFF from operations and reinvestment

Begin with a cash-operating surplus before income taxes and financing. Under the clean accounting bridge used here, this is EBIT + D&A − ΔW. Subtract the cash tax the operating business would pay without interest deductions, denoted TU, and cash capital expenditure:

FCFFt = EBITt + D&At − TUt − CapExt − ΔWt.

If taxable operating profit equals EBIT, tax is paid immediately, the rate τ is constant and applicable, and there are no losses, credits or temporary differences, then TU = τ EBIT. Define after-tax operating profit NOPAT = EBIT(1−τ). The familiar compact formula follows:

Net reinvestment Rt = CapExt − D&At + ΔWt.
FCFFt = NOPATt − Rt = EBITt(1−τ) + D&At − CapExt − ΔWt.

When there are no disposals, revaluations, acquisitions or other stock changes, operating invested capital K = net operating fixed assets + W satisfies Kt − Kt−1 = Rt. This is a stock-flow check, not a claim that accounting depreciation always measures economic wear. A business winding down can release capital and have negative R. A growing business generally cannot sustain rising cash forever merely by assuming that no additional investment is needed; the next chapter develops that economic constraint.

For a real forecast, reconcile cash taxes explicitly. Deferred tax expense is not a current payment; a loss carryforward is not automatically an immediate refund. Also adjust unusual noncash charges and nonoperating income rather than mechanically adding every reported noncash item forever. For example, equity compensation transfers an ownership claim even when no cash salary leaves the company. Its cost cannot disappear from both the cash forecast and the ownership analysis.

3. Derive FCFE and locate the interest tax shield

Let I be cash interest and B net borrowing: new debt proceeds minus cash principal repayments. With no issue premium, fees or remeasurement, B = Dt−Dt−1, where D is debt principal. In the simple current-tax case, net income NI = (EBIT−I)(1−τ). Starting after interest and tax gives:

FCFEt = NIt + D&At − CapExt − ΔWt + Bt
= FCFFt − It(1−τ) + Bt.

The second line follows by substituting NI = EBIT(1−τ)−I(1−τ). Equivalently, FCFF = NI + I(1−τ) + D&A − CapEx − ΔW. If a reconstructed operating cash-flow measure includes interest and the stated current taxes, then FCFE = CFO − CapEx + B and FCFF = CFO + I(1−τ) − CapEx. Published CFO may classify interest differently or contain other adjustments, so establish the cash-flow boundary before using this shortcut.

More generally let TL be cash tax with the actual financing and let S = TU−TL be the period's cash interest-tax saving. Holding the operating path fixed gives FCFE = FCFF − I + S + B. Only under the immediate full-deduction assumptions does S = τI. A cap on deductions, delayed tax payment or unusable loss can break that shortcut. When NI contains different book tax, reconstruct cash tax as in Volume 7 before using the cash equation.

This also settles a subtle reconciliation. Net cash to lenders is I−B, so FCFE + net lender cash = FCFF + S. Our FCFF is based on unlevered taxes; the actual levered business can distribute the additional tax saving. Calling FCFF “cash to all investors” without stating this convention can hide that difference. Jenter's MIT WACC/APV notes distinguish operating free cash flow that excludes interest tax shields from methods that value the financing benefit.

FCFE is a potential net shareholder cash flow under an operating and financing plan, not an instruction to pay a dividend. It may be retained, repurchased, distributed or needed to build a cash reserve. A valuation using FCFE must account for eventual shareholder access and any required new equity consistently. Our worked firm pays all positive FCFE and retains no cash, so its shareholder cash is directly observable within the model. A bank, regulated entity or business with material restricted cash needs a different explicit construction.

4. Build one complete operating and financing path

Worked example 1 — Cedar's two-year cash claims

Cedar Service Runoff is an original fictional service business. Money is kCU. Date 0 is 31 December 2026, date 1 is 31 December 2027 and date 2 is 31 December 2028. These are hypothetical dated inputs, not observed future results. Value the company at date 0 immediately after any date-0 distributions. Every modeled cash payment occurs at the stated year-end. Receivables are the only operating working-capital balance; there is no inventory or payable. Opening cash is zero, receivables 8.5 and net equipment 40, financed by debt 40 and book equity 8.5.

The service contracts end at date 2. Old equipment is depreciated 25 in year 1 and 15 in year 2; new equipment bought for 10 at date 1 serves only year 2 and is fully depreciated then. Thus total depreciation is 25 in each year. At date 2 every receivable has been collected, equipment has no sale or continuing service value, and no future cash remains. Zero continuation follows from these explicit facts, not merely from zero book value.

All ordinary costs and income taxes are paid in the year. Book and tax depreciation agree; income remains taxable and interest deductions are fully used at the supplied tax rate 25%. Debt pays 5% on opening principal; repayment occurs after interest at the year-end. Principal falls from 40 to 20 to zero. No fees, defaults, new shares, other claims or cash retention occur. Shareholders receive all available equity cash.

Cedar inputs and operating bridge, kCU
ItemYear 1Year 2
Revenue / cash operating costs322 / 175249 / 125
D&A / CapEx25 / 1025 / 0
Ending receivables / change in W5.5 / −30 / −5.5
EBIT / unlevered cash tax122 / 30.599 / 24.75
NOPAT / net reinvestment91.5 / −1874.25 / −30.5
FCFF109.5104.75

Year 1 FCFF is 122×0.75 + 25 − 10 − (−3) = 109.5. Operating capital falls from 48.5 to 25+5.5 = 30.5: the decrease 18 matches net reinvestment −18. Year 2 FCFF is 99×0.75 + 25 − 0 − (−5.5) = 104.75, and the remaining 30.5 of capital is released. This is a runoff, so the releases are finite and do not establish a recurring growth margin.

Interest is 2 in year 1 and 1 in year 2. Actual cash taxes are (122−2)×25% = 30 and (99−1)×25% = 24.5. NI is therefore 90 and 73.5. The tax savings relative to the unlevered calculation are 0.5 and 0.25. With net borrowing −20 each year, FCFE is 109.5−2×0.75−20 = 88, then 104.75−1×0.75−20 = 84.

Independent receipts, cash and closing-account checks, kCU
CheckYear 1Year 2
Receipts = revenue − ΔW325254.5
Direct CFO = receipts − operating costs − interest − actual tax325−175−2−30 = 118254.5−125−1−24.5 = 104
Indirect CFO = NI + D&A − ΔW90+25+3 = 11873.5+25+5.5 = 104
CFO − CapEx + B − shareholder payment118−10−20−88 = 0104−0−20−84 = 0
Ending equipment / receivables / cash25 / 5.5 / 00 / 0 / 0
Ending debt / book equity20 / 10.50 / 0

Book equity follows 8.5+90−88 = 10.5 and then 10.5+73.5−84 = 0. Lenders receive interest plus principal of 22 and 21. Total investor cash is 88+22 = 110 and 84+21 = 105, exactly FCFF plus the corresponding tax saving. None of these reconciliations uses a balancing cash plug.

5. Reconcile operating, debt and equity values

For a claim with year-end cash Ct and compatible one-period required returns rt, its date-0 value is Σ Ct/Πs=1…t(1+rs), plus any consistently timed residual claim. Under a constant rate this becomes Σ Ct/(1+r)t. A changing annual rate uses the cumulative product, not (1+rt)t. The rate belongs to the risk and units of the claim, not to the label on the spreadsheet tab.

Worked example 2 — Two routes to the same ordinary equity

For this example alone, all Cedar operating cash, tax benefits and contractual debt payments are certain, freely transferable and priced at the same supplied effective annual return of 5%. There are no personal taxes or transaction frictions. Debt and equity both require 5% because neither claim is risky in this construction; this is not a general statement about leveraged shares.

Let Vt, Dt and Et be market values immediately after date-t cash distributions and principal changes. V is the value of the remaining operating business with its financing tax benefits; no separate cash or nonoperating asset is present. At date 2 all values are zero. At date 1 the remaining investor cash is 105, so V1 = 105/1.05 = 100. At date 0, V0 = (110+100)/1.05 = 200. These are market values of future claims, not the 48.5 and 30.5 accounting capital balances.

Debt is at par: D0 = 22/1.05 + 21/1.05² = 40, D1 = 21/1.05 = 20. Consequently E0 = 200−40 = 160 and E1 = 100−20 = 80. Direct shareholder valuation agrees: 88/1.05 + 84/1.05² = 160. The one-period checks are (88+80)/1.05 = 160 and 84/1.05 = 80. Date-1 value 80 excludes the 88 just paid; adding that payment again would mix before- and after-distribution values.

We can also discount FCFF, which excluded interest tax savings. Both opening market debt weights are 20%: 40/200 and 20/100. With kE = kD = 5% and immediately usable τ = 25%, the compatible after-tax weighted average cost of capital is:

WACC = [E/(D+E)]kE + [D/(D+E)]kD(1−τ)
= 0.80×5% + 0.20×5%×0.75 = 4.75%.

The cash recursion confirms its use rather than merely assuming it: 104.75/1.0475 = 100, and (109.5+100)/1.0475 = 200. Thus FCFF discounted at 4.75% gives operating value 200; subtract date-0 debt 40 once to get equity 160. After valuing FCFE directly at its 5% rate, debt must not be subtracted again.

An explicit financing-benefit check is also possible because every claim is certain here. Discount unlevered FCFF at 5%: its value is 87,890/441 ≈ 199.2971. Discount the separate tax savings at 5%: 0.5/1.05 + 0.25/1.05² = 310/441 ≈ 0.7029. Their sum is 200. This is an elementary adjusted-present-value calculation. Either include the benefit through the compatible FCFF discount rate, or value it separately at a justified rate. Adding it to the already shield-adjusted 200 counts it twice.

The WACC expression is conditional. Changing the debt schedule changes interest, available shields and market weights; under risk, it can change the shareholder required return too. A constant book debt ratio or a fixed amount borrowed today does not establish a constant market debt ratio thereafter. The MIT notes' discussion of changing leverage motivates using an explicit financing valuation when that policy changes. Chapter 4 supplies the risk and rate-estimation tools; Exercise 8 isolates the policy issue even in a certain world.

6. State what the operating value includes

“Enterprise value” and “firm value” are sometimes used loosely. Here Vop is the value obtained from the specified operating FCFF and compatible financing treatment. When operating flows exclude excess-cash income and other investments, ordinary-equity value at the same date is:

Eordinary = Vop + value of separately excluded cash/nonoperating assets − market value of debt − value of other senior or outside-owner claims.

For example, operating value 500, separately available excess cash 30, another investment worth 20 and debt worth 160 imply ordinary equity 390 when there are no other claims. Required operating cash already modeled in the operating investment path is not another free asset to add. A pension or lease obligation already represented by future operating payments must not also be deducted in full without undoing the corresponding cash-flow treatment. If a forecast includes 100% of a subsidiary's operations, the parent-shareholder bridge must account for the outside owners' claim. Market claim values, historical book balances and contractual face amounts are different concepts; Cedar's debt happens to trade at par under its supplied certain-rate contract.

A dividend changes timing: immediately before a known distribution q, the cum-distribution equity claim includes q; immediately afterward its value excludes q, with other information and tax effects held fixed. If cash is 30 after the dividend and the valuation is also after it, subtracting that dividend a second time is wrong. Similarly, purchasing an existing operating business does not mean subtracting its historical equipment cost again from a DCF of future net cash. An acquisition price is the new investor's date-0 outlay used to calculate that investor's NPV.

7. Match nominal cash to nominal rates

A nominal cash amount is measured in the currency units paid at its date. A real cash amount uses the purchasing power of a stated base date. Let the relevant price index be P0 = 1. With a known constant inflation rate π, Pt = (1+π)t, nominal cash CNt = PtCRt, and compatible gross discount rates satisfy:

1+rN = (1+rR)(1+π).
CNt/(1+rN)t = CRt/(1+rR)t.

The equality follows by canceling the price-index factors. Adding the real rate and inflation is only an approximation; it omits their product. For varying known inflation use the product of the successive gross inflation factors and match the discount curve period by period. Damodaran's consistency discussion distinguishes real and nominal cash and notes that a claim safe in nominal units need not be safe in purchasing power.

Worked example 3 — Purchasing power and currency conversion

First consider a separate claim paying 60 and 90 in date-0 purchasing-power kCU at dates 1 and 2. Known inflation is 4% annually; the supplied real rate is 5%. Nominal cash is 60×1.04 = 62.4 and 90×1.04² = 97.344. The compatible nominal rate is 1.05×1.04−1 = 9.2%, not 9%. Both valuations are:

60/1.05 + 90/1.05² = 62.4/1.092 + 97.344/1.092² = 6,800/49 ≈ 138.7755.

Inflating the cash and retaining the 5% rate would overvalue these positive payments. But an actual contract that promises a fixed nominal 60 does not become 62.4 merely because prices rise. Classify the quoted amount first. Where tax depreciation remains fixed in nominal units, forecast the actual nominal tax cash first; simply inflating every accounting expense could change the tax law implicitly.

Now use a different claim, denominated in fictional foreign currency F: it pays 105 and 110.25 kF. Its certain nominal F rate is 5%. Home currency H has a supplied certain nominal rate of 8%, and date-0 exchange is 2 H per F. The known hypothetical date-1 and date-2 conversion rates are 72/35 and 2,592/1,225 H per F. They were chosen to match these discount rates: St = 2×(1.08/1.05)t.

Convert at each payment's date: the H cash amounts are 216 and 233.28 kH. Foreign PV is 105/1.05 + 110.25/1.05² = 200 kF. Home PV is 216/1.08 + 233.28/1.08² = 400 kH, agreeing with 2 H/F × 200 kF. Discounting the unchanged foreign numbers at the lower or higher home rate would mix units. Converting every future cash flow at today's spot while keeping these different discount rates would describe a different exchange path.

The nominal-real identity above is exact for the supplied known price path and matching rates. It is not a general rule that subtracting expected inflation from a risky nominal expected return produces an exact real discount rate. Random inflation can covary with payoffs and purchasing-power risk. Keep uncertain operating scenarios, inflation exposure and the rate model consistent instead of hiding the difference in a rounding adjustment.

8. Match the currency path and discount curve

Write St explicitly as home units per foreign unit. Multiplying foreign cash by St gives home cash. In the certain frictionless example, St = S0[(1+rH)/(1+rF)]t, so direct substitution gives StCFt/(1+rH)t = S0CFt/(1+rF)t. It is a transparent unit-and-price consistency check. We have stipulated known conversion and borrowing/lending conditions; the equation is not an empirical prediction of future spot rates.

For uncertain exchange rates, a forward exchange rate is not automatically an unbiased expected future spot rate. Also E[StCFt] = E[St]E[CFt] + Cov(St, CFt); the product of two forecasts can omit covariance. Tax on remittances, transfer restrictions and hedging costs can change the accessible cash claim. A business's headquarters do not determine the currency rate: the unit in which the claim is forecast does. The cited consistency source supports matching currency and rate; our known-path example makes no broader purchasing-power-parity claim.

9. Put continuation value at the correct date

A forecast horizon H is a modeling boundary, not necessarily the business's death. Define TVH as the date-H value after the explicit date-H payment of all remaining cash from H+1 onward. Then:

V0 = Σt=1…H Ct/(1+r)t + TVH/(1+r)H.

If the remaining positive cash begins at CH+1 and grows forever at constant g, with constant compatible r, r > −1 and −1 < g < r, its date-H geometric series is [CH+1/(1+r)] Σj=0…∞[(1+g)/(1+r)]j. The ratio has magnitude below one, giving TVH = CH+1/(r−g). With positive cash and g ≥ r, this series does not produce a finite positive value; a zero or negative denominator is not an alternative valuation shortcut. The terminal-value derivation discussion likewise places next-period cash in the numerator and requires stable assumptions.

Worked example 4 — A date-2 continuation claim

A separate operating business has explicit FCFF 30 at date 1 and 36 at date 2. Supplied date-3 FCFF is 40 after all required reinvestment, then grows 2% forever. The compatible constant operating rate is 10%; the continued operating and financing conditions are assumptions to investigate, not results of the division. Thus TV2 = 40/(0.10−0.02) = 500. The date-0 operating value is:

30/1.10 + (36+500)/1.10² = 56,900/121 ≈ 470.2479.

The explicit payments contribute 6,900/121 ≈ 57.0248; the continuation contributes 50,000/121 ≈ 413.2231. The large continuation share makes evidence about the continuing business important. Do not grow the already supplied next-period 40 again. Do not use 36 in its place. Do not discount TV2 for three years, and do not add a second release of all working capital while also assuming the same business continues operating.

If operating continuation value is 500, separately excluded excess cash at date 2 is 20 and the debt claim remaining then is worth 100, the ordinary-equity continuation claim is 420 in a firm with no other claims. This 420 belongs in a compatible equity valuation. It is not interchangeable with operating TV 500; neither is an extra operating payment. If debt is instead repaid at date 2, use the resulting post-repayment balances and cash consistently.

A finite liquidation model instead includes actual after-tax sale proceeds, collection of working capital and settlement costs, with no invented continuation. Cedar already includes final collection and complete debt repayment in date-2 cash, so TV2 = 0. Growth, reinvestment, competitive fade and sustainable terminal operating assumptions receive full treatment in Chapter 3. Their credibility cannot be inferred merely from g being less than r.

10. Reproduce and interrogate the cash bridge

Download the original inputs and contract, complete standard-library program and execution and benchmark guide into one directory. Run python3 v08-c02-analysis.py, optionally followed by a replacement input path. It prints exact JSON without network access or file writes. Fractions such as 19/400 mean 4.75%, not 19%. The lab derives values from the certain investor cash first and then checks the implied FCFF rates; it never imposes a constant rate after the debt policy changes.

Inspect operating capital, current tax, debt principal, book equity, cash payments and the market-value bridge separately. The model rejects unsupported losses, negative required shareholder funding and a nonzero ending runoff balance. Those cases need new economic contracts rather than forced zeroes. Source inspection supports the methods; it does not verify Cedar's fictional business or turn supplied rates into market estimates.

Exercises

  1. Derive and diagnose. Under the chapter's simple current-tax assumptions, derive FCFF from NI and derive FCFE from FCFF. An analyst asserts “FCFF equals FCFE plus gross interest minus net borrowing.” Identify the missing term. Explain why neither positive FCFE nor a depreciation addback proves that cash can safely be distributed; distinguish a payment to owners from cash retained for them.
  2. A new one-year reconciliation. A fictional firm begins with zero cash, receivables 10, net equipment 80, debt 80 and book equity 10, all in kCU. Revenue is 240, cash operating costs 150, depreciation 20 and capex 35. Ending receivables are 18. Debt charges 10% on opening principal; a new 12 is borrowed at year-end. Tax is 25% of positive EBIT less interest, paid currently; unlevered tax uses EBIT. All positive FCFE is paid. Calculate EBIT, NOPAT, NI, receipts, direct/indirect CFO, FCFF, FCFE and the closing balance sheet. Show what changes in the cash claims if no new borrowing is available and all other operating inputs remain fixed.
  3. A restricted cash tax shield. EBIT is 80, depreciation 20, capex 30, ΔW is 5, interest is 10 and net borrowing is −8. Supplied tax schedules give unlevered cash tax 18 and levered cash tax 17; actual income tax expense also equals 17. All amounts are kCU. Calculate FCFF, NI, CFO and FCFE using both cash routes. A proposed shortcut uses statutory τ = 25% in I(1−τ). Quantify its error and identify the further evidence needed before forecasting a future deduction benefit.
  4. Same-date value bridge. An operating DCF of fully consolidated activities is 650 kCU. It already includes the investment and benefits of required operating cash 11. Separately excluded, accessible excess cash is 35 and a nonoperating investment is worth 25. Debt's market value is 180 (book value 150), preferred claims are worth 40, outside owners of consolidated subsidiaries hold claims worth 30, and a separate obligation worth 20 has cash payments excluded from the operating forecast. There are 22 thousand ordinary shares. All values and the excess-cash amount are immediately after a dividend of 10 has already been paid. Compute ordinary equity and value per share; explain the treatment of required cash, book debt and the dividend.
  5. Nominal-real transfer. A certain claim pays 100 kCU in date-0 purchasing power at both year-ends. Known inflation is 2% per year and the real required rate is 5%. Derive the nominal cash and exact nominal rate, show equal present values, and calculate the overstatement from discounting the nominal cash at 5%. State why this does not license automatic inflation of a fixed nominal contractual payment.
  6. Currency transfer. Certain foreign payments are 110 and 121 kF at dates 1 and 2, with foreign rate 10%. The home rate is 4% and date-0 exchange is 3 H per F. Use the known path St = 3(1.04/1.10)t. Compute both future exchange rates, converted home cash and both present values. Explain why lowering the discount rate without converting the cash is invalid, and name the additional term omitted by multiplying separate expected exchange-rate and cash-flow forecasts under uncertainty.
  7. Continuation timing. Explicit operating cash is 12 at date 1 and 15 at date 2; supplied date-3 cash after reinvestment is 18. The compatible constant rate is 8% and perpetual growth is 2%. Calculate TV2 and date-0 value. Write the first two terms of the date-2 continuation series. Explain what fails if someone sets perpetual growth to 8%, and why ending the explicit forecast at date 2 does not justify a full working-capital release in addition to a going-concern TV.
  8. A financing-policy challenge. Keep all Cedar operating inputs and the certain 5% rate, but leave debt at 40 through date 1 and repay all 40 at date 2. Recompute interest, cash shields and FCFE, then value the equity and the operating business. Is the original constant 4.75% FCFF rate still compatible? Establish the date-1 market debt weight and show the changed rate there. Evaluate “FCFF has not changed, so financing cannot have affected value” without asserting that ever more debt would be optimal in an actual risky business.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. NI = (EBIT−I)(1−τ), so EBIT(1−τ) = NI + I(1−τ). Adding depreciation and subtracting investment gives FCFF = NI + I(1−τ) + D&A − CapEx − ΔW. Starting from the actual shareholder residual adds net borrowing and deducts the financing cash: FCFE = FCFF − I(1−τ) + B. The asserted inverse omits the cash tax saving: FCFE + I − B = FCFF + τI, not FCFF. With imperfect current tax use, replace τI by the actual S = TU−TL.

    Positive FCFE is conditional on the investment, financing and cash-reserve assumptions; it does not establish legal permission, lender consent or daily liquidity. Depreciation is reversal of a noncash charge, while equipment may require a separate replacement payment. A dividend or repurchase actually transfers cash; retained cash remains an asset whose accessible future benefit must be valued. Full credit requires the algebra, the tax convention and both distribution distinctions, rather than only memorized formulas.

  2. EBIT = 240−150−20 = 70; NOPAT = 70×0.75 = 52.5. Interest is 8, levered tax 15.5 and NI = 46.5. Receipts are 240+10−18 = 232. Direct CFO = 232−150−8−15.5 = 58.5; indirect CFO = 46.5+20−8 = 58.5. FCFF = 52.5+20−35−8 = 29.5. FCFE = 58.5−35+12 = 35.5, also 29.5−8×0.75+12.

    Closing equipment is 80+35−20 = 95, receivables 18 and cash zero: assets 113. Debt is 92; equity is 10+46.5−35.5 = 21; total claims are 113. Cash reconciles as 58.5−35+12−35.5 = 0. Without the new loan, FCFF and this year's interest, tax, NI and CFO are unchanged under the final-date borrowing convention. FCFE falls to 23.5; if paid, debt stays 80 and closing book equity becomes 33, still totaling 113. Borrowing changes the residual and claims, not the current operating cash created.

  3. Use the supplied cash tax, not an invented proportional deduction. FCFF = 80−18+20−30−5 = 47. NI = 80−10−17 = 53; CFO = 53+20−5 = 68. Thus FCFE = 68−30−8 = 30. The current shield is S = 18−17 = 1, and the other route gives 47−10+1−8 = 30.

    The shortcut gives 47−10×0.75−8 = 31.5, an overstatement of 1.5, because it assumes a current shield of 2.5. A possible later benefit needs the actual deduction rule, limits, carryforward expiry, future taxable income and payment timing; its future existence, amount and discount rate are not supplied here. The calculation alone does not establish a permanently lost or guaranteed deferred benefit.

  4. Ordinary equity = 650+35+25−180−40−30−20 = 440 kCU. Dividing by 22 thousand shares gives 20 CU per share. Adding the required cash 11 again duplicates an asset already represented in operations. Use the supplied debt market claim 180, not book 150. The outside owners' claim is deducted because the operating DCF includes their share of consolidated activities. The separate obligation is deducted because its payments were expressly excluded; if they had already reduced cash flow, a second full deduction would need adjustment. The dividend has already left and every balance is after it; subtracting 10 again misstates the valuation date.

  5. The nominal amounts are 102 and 104.04; rN = 1.05×1.02−1 = 7.1%. Both 100/1.05 + 100/1.05² and 102/1.071 + 104.04/1.071² equal 82,000/441 ≈ 185.9410. The mismatched value is 102/1.05 + 104.04/1.05² = 9,384/49 ≈ 191.5102; the overstatement is 2,456/441 ≈ 5.5692. A fixed nominal 100 remains 100 nominal; its real value falls with inflation. The example inflates payments expressly quoted in constant purchasing power.

  6. S1 = 156/55 ≈ 2.83636 H/F, S2 = 8,112/3,025 ≈ 2.68165 H/F. Home cash is 110×156/55 = 312 and 121×8,112/3,025 = 324.48 kH. Foreign PV = 110/1.10 + 121/1.10² = 200 kF; home PV = 312/1.04 + 324.48/1.04² = 600 kH, exactly 3×200. Here the home currency strengthens along the supplied path. The numerical size of a rate cannot be separated from the unit and cash path. Under uncertainty the omitted term is Cov(St, CFt), with an appropriate risk-pricing model also needed.

  7. TV2 = 18/(0.08−0.02) = 300. The first date-2 series terms are 18/1.08 and (18×1.02)/1.08²; they are future dates 3 and 4 viewed from date 2. Date-0 value = 12/1.08 + (15+300)/1.08² = 22,775/81 ≈ 281.1728. The explicit payments contribute 5,825/243 and continuation 62,500/243. At g = r the positive discounted terms do not shrink and their sum diverges; dividing by zero cannot value the claim. A continuing business still needs its modeled operating capital. Only a specified liquidation or genuine surplus release supports a separate release, with the continuation assumptions adjusted accordingly.

  8. Year 1 interest and shield stay 2 and 0.5; year 2 interest becomes 2 and its shield 0.5. Net borrowing is 0 then −40. FCFE becomes 109.5−2×0.75 = 108, then 104.75−2×0.75−40 = 63.25. Equity PV is 108/1.05 + 63.25/1.05² = 70,660/441 ≈ 160.2268. Debt remains worth 40 at date 0, so operating value with these financing benefits is 88,300/441 ≈ 200.2268.

    At date 1, V1 = (104.75+0.5)/1.05 = 2,105/21 ≈ 100.2381, and E1 = 1,265/21. The opening year-2 debt weight is 40/(2,105/21) = 168/421 ≈ 39.905%. Its compatible WACC is 5%[1−0.25×168/421] = 379/8,420 ≈ 4.5012%; year 1's compatible rate is 8,389/176,600 ≈ 4.7503%. Use the product of these period factors. The old constant 4.75% would still value the unchanged FCFF at 200 and miss the 100/441 ≈ 0.2268 extra value of the additional date-2 shield 0.25. Financing changed a tax payment even though unlevered FCFF did not change.

    This result relies on supplied certain profits, immediate deductions, certain debt service and no distress or other financing costs. It does not establish an optimal real leverage policy. A convincing critique identifies the tax effect, changed market weights and discounting rule without hiding the inconsistency in a new cash-flow plug.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back. Explain Cedar's 90 NI, 118 CFO, 109.5 FCFF and 88 shareholder cash to a colleague, including why the two valuation rates differ. Answer: NI has already deducted depreciation, interest and actual tax. Add back depreciation 25 and release receivables 3 to get CFO 118. Deduct capex 10 and debt repayment 20 to obtain shareholder cash 88. For FCFF, replace actual financing treatment with unlevered tax: add after-tax interest 1.5 to CFO and deduct capex 10, giving 109.5. Actual combined lender/shareholder cash is 110 because of the 0.5 interest-tax saving. The certain investor claims require 5%; the compatible 4.75% FCFF rate incorporates the shield under the demonstrated 20% market debt policy. Full credit requires both the cash bridge and the financing assumption.

Delayed check. Without changing Cedar sales, costs, tax rules or the original 40→20→0 debt schedule, delay collection of 5 from date 1 to date 2. Date-1 receivables become 10.5; final receivables stay zero. Find each FCFF and FCFE and the change in date-0 equity value. Answer: NI and tax are unchanged. FCFF becomes 104.5 and 109.75; FCFE becomes 83 and 89. Moving 5 one year later reduces equity value by 5/1.05−5/1.05² = 100/441 ≈ 0.2268. New equity value is 70,460/441 ≈ 159.7732. The total cash is unchanged but its timing is less valuable. Since market values changed while the debt amounts did not, do not silently preserve the original constant market debt weight or 4.75% WACC; the certain shareholder rate remains 5% by the stated contract.

Sources and next step

The primary references support cash-claim definitions, separate or rate-based treatment of financing benefits, currency and purchasing-power consistency, and next-period continuation timing. Their historical examples, market figures and broader claims are not evidence about today's markets. All chapter data, derivations, exercises and code are original. Next, connect cash generation to investment returns and sustainable growth in Chapter 3, then estimate risk-matched required returns in Chapter 4. A reconciled valuation is the beginning of economic scrutiny, not proof that its operating or financing assumptions will occur.

Sources and further study

  • Aswath Damodaran, Financial Measures and Ratios — FCFF, FCFE and noncash working-capital entries — Scoped definitions of unlevered-tax operating cash, equity cash after net borrowing, reinvestment and noncash operating working capital; entity/claim distinctions. Cedar numbers and derivations are original. Unrelated ratio, historical accounting and tax generalizations on the page are not adopted.
  • Dirk Jenter, MIT 15.402 Finance Theory II, WACC and APV (Spring 2003) — Operating free cash flow excludes interest-tax shields; compatible WACC and separately valued financing effects are alternative routes. Market leverage and policy stability qualify a constant WACC. The chapter's original all-certain finite model does not use the lecture's risk estimates or examples.
  • Aswath Damodaran, Riskfree Rates — Cash Flow Consistency and Real versus Nominal Rates — Match the cash-flow currency and nominal/real unit with the discount-rate construction; distinguish nominal certainty from purchasing-power certainty. Chapter currency-path equalities are original deterministic consistency demonstrations, not a general purchasing-power-parity prediction.
  • Aswath Damodaran, Applied Corporate Finance Chapter 12 — Discussion Issues and Derivations — Consistency of firm/equity valuation; continuation value uses the next cash flow at the horizon and stable rate/growth assumptions; reinvestment must support the cash path. The chapter supplies its own geometric-series proof and original examples, deferring economic growth/fade analysis to c03.
